To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the slow negative shift of the cortical potential is a reflection of the depolarization potential of the cortical astrocytes.

the slow cortical negativity is mainly the result of depolarization of cortical glial cells, whereas the inhibitory postsynptatic potentials of cortical neurons play a much lesser role in the generation of this negativity.

the slow negativity of the cortical surface is a reflection of glial depolarizing response and the negative shift is a reflection of depolarizing and hyperpolarizing responses of glia and neuronal elements respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the contribution of glia and nerve cells to the surface-negative potential of the cerebral cortex and to the negative shift of this potential during its high-frequency stimulation.
the mechanisms of the generation of the surface-negative potentials during electrical stimulation of the cerebral cortex.
the contribution of glial and neuronal components of cortical surface-negative potentials to the negative shift of potential.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the slow negativity of the cortical surface potential is a reflection of the depolarization and the negative shift--of the depolarization or hyperpolarization.

the surface-negative shift of the potential evoked by high-frequency stimulation is the result of the depolarization and hyperpolarization shifts of the membrane potentials of cortical glial and neuronal cells, respectively, and the surface-negative potential evoked by a single stimulus is the result of depolarization and the hyperpolarizing inhibitory postsynptotic potential of glia and neuronal cells, the depolarization being the basic component of the potential.
glial cells are the main source of the slow negative potentials on the cortical surface and in the cortical intercellular cisternae.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surface-negative potentials are generated by glial cells.
glial depolarizations play a significant role in the formation of surface-negative potentials.
the negative shift of potential is mainly a result of the accumulation of K+ in the intercellular cifts, and the basic component of this accumulation is the K+ released from the glial cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glial cells play an active role in the genesis of the slow negativity of the cortical surface.
the surface negative potentials of the cerebral cortical electrical stimulation reflect mainly the depolarizing shift of the cortical glia.
glial cells play a major role in the generation of the surface-negative potentials during stimulation of the cerebral cortex.
